newsitem.title: USA: US Prods Outlook - Heat seen livelier on cold snap.
newsitem.headline: US Prods Outlook - Heat seen livelier on cold snap.

text.p: Heating oil trade is likely to dominate the U.S. products market activity this week, as players prepare to supplement inventories ahead of the coldest weather of the season.

Activity in the heating oil cash markets should increase after prices rallied six cents from last week's lows, traders said, helped by technical factors in the futures market and forecasts of far-colder-than-normal weather in the Midwest and East Coast.
Seasonal fundamentals should move to the forefront, with gasoline stocks deemed ample by the trade and the bullish weather horizon for the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.
"With the cold front coming in, we should see more emphasis on the distillates," said Paulo Nery, senior consultant with Pace Consultants Inc of Houston.
In early Monday action on the NYMEX, January heating oil jumped 3.0 cents, while January gasoline rallied about 1.5 cents.
As many as three waves of cold Arctic air will descend on the U.S. east of the Rocky Mountains in December, Smith Barney weather forecaster Jon Davis reported Friday.
The cold snap, which may remain through the end of December, will push temperatures in the eastern third of the country 12 to 18 degrees (Fahrenheit) below normal levels, Davis predicted.
Distillate output on the U.S. East Coast remains well below year-ago levels, Nery added, and is likely to contribute to the renewed interest in heating oil trade.
Lending firm support are American Petroleum Institute data showing heating oil stocks in the East Coast about 28 percent below last year's levels.
But that interest in heating oil may be only a temporary phenemenon, since weather concerns only recently moved to the forefront of the market.
"It's hard to say how long these things last," one East Coast trader said.
"There's still a fair number of sellers in the Gulf" trying to move heating oil before the end of the year, the trader said, which could keep prices from moving sharply higher.
The shift in focus to the heating oil market should come at the expense of gasoline, according to traders, following last week's choppy trading.

Outright New York Harbor prices for conventional unleaded "M5"-grade barrels saw a modest bounce Thursday and Friday, helping offset about a third of the ten-cent losses made over the previous two weeks.
Gasoline activity may also become subdued as buyers seemed likely to back off amid increased imports in the harbor.
Between about 500,000 and 1.5 million barrels of gasoline will arrive in NYH by the end of December, which should be more than adequate to meet the near-term demand, traders said.
-- Matt Daily, New York Energy Desk 1 212 859 1620
